intro: Angels are everywhere in modern life: on greeting cards, in movies, on holiday trees and in everyday sayings. Most of those pictures come from centuries of art and tradition. This unit goes back to the texts themselves. You will read what the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament and other ancient Jewish writings actually say about the beings they call angels, cherubim, seraphim, watchers and holy ones.

Each lesson starts from an ancient text: Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, the Gospels, Revelation, the Greek Septuagint, 1 Enoch, Jubilees, Tobit, Josephus and the Dead Sea Scrolls. Then you will hear how researchers read it. Michael S. Heiser, in Angels (2018), argued that some terms describe a being's role, such as messenger, and others its status, such as elohim. E. Theodore Mullen, J. T. Milik, George Nickelsburg, Carol Newsom, Clinton Arnold and Walter Wink add other angles.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain the main words for heavenly beings and where they appear. You will be able to tell what a text says from what later writers and artists added. You will also be able to explain why the texts insist that angels serve God and are never to be worshiped, and how different traditions read those texts.
bigQuestion: What do the ancient texts really say about angels, and how can a careful reader tell that apart from what later traditions added?

test.q: The Hebrew mal'ak and the Greek angelos both mean what?
test.why: Both words mean messenger. They name a job, which is why Genesis 32 uses mal'ak for heavenly and human messengers alike.

test.q: Which Hebrew word can name the God of Israel and the members of his council?
test.why: Psalm 82:1 uses elohim for both. Heiser read it as a word for any being of the spirit world.

test.q: In which book does Nebuchadnezzar dream of a watcher and a holy one?
test.why: Daniel 4:13 and 4:17 describe the watchers and holy ones in the king's dream.

test.q: What do the cherubim do in Genesis 3:24 and Exodus 25?
choices: Guard the space where God is present
test.why: Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life and cover the ark, where God meets Moses.

test.q: Which beings have six wings in Isaiah 6?
test.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

test.q: Where does the idea of nine ranked choirs of angels come from?
choices: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
test.why: Pseudo-Dionysius arranged nine orders about 500 CE. Paul names some powers without ranking them.

test.q: Which two angels are named in the Protestant Bible?
test.why: Only Michael and Gabriel are named in the Protestant Bible. Raphael appears in Tobit.

test.q: Which verse lists angels and the spirits of just men as separate groups?
test.why: Hebrews 12:22-23 names the company of angels and the spirits of just men side by side.

test.q: Hebrews 1:6 quotes a line about angels worshiping the Son. Which form of Deuteronomy 32:43 does it match?
test.why: The line matches the Greek Septuagint; a Dead Sea Scrolls copy has a similar Hebrew line.

test.q: In Revelation 22:8-9, why does the angel refuse John's worship?
choices: John has not yet been cleansed
He wants to be called by name
He is a fellow servant, and worship belongs to God
He is not allowed to speak
test.why: The angel calls himself John's fellow servant and says, "worship God."

test.q: Stephen, Paul and the writer of Hebrews all say the law was given with the help of whom?
test.why: Acts 7:53, Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2 all speak of angels at the giving of the law.

test.q: Which statement about Colossians 2:18 is accurate?

test.why: The phrase may mean worship given to angels or joining in the angels' own worship.

test.q: In the birth stories, how does the angel speak to Joseph?
test.why: Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19 describe the angel speaking to Joseph in dreams.

test.q: Which reading of the empty-tomb accounts fits them together into one fuller story?
test.why: Harmonizing combines the Gospel accounts into one story and explains differences as different focus.

test.q: Which popular idea is not found in the Bible's texts?
choices: People become angels when they die
test.why: The texts keep angels and humans distinct; Hebrews 12:22-23 lists them as separate groups. The dead do not become angels.

title: Angels Up Close

chapters.title: Names, Ranks and Roles
chapters.bigQuestion: When the Bible names heavenly beings, is it describing what they are, what they do, or where they stand?

story.title: Holy, Holy, Holy
story.kicker: In the year a king died, the prophet Isaiah says he saw the LORD enthroned, with burning beings calling out above him.
paragraphs: Isaiah 6 opens with a date. "In the year that king Uzziah died," Isaiah says, he saw the LORD sitting on a throne, high and lifted up. Uzziah had ruled Judah for decades, and his death is usually dated around 740 BCE. A long reign had ended. The prophet's vision begins at a moment of change for his people.

In the vision, the hem of the LORD's robe fills the temple. Above him stand seraphim. Each has six wings. With two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they fly. They call to one another: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." The doorposts shake, and the house fills with smoke.

Isaiah does not feel ready. He is shaken. He says he is a man of unclean lips, living among a people of unclean lips. Then one of the seraphim flies to him with a live coal from the altar. It touches his mouth, and the seraph tells him his guilt is taken away. The scene moves from fear to cleansing.

Then a voice asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me." Many scholars read the word "us" as God speaking in front of his heavenly council, like the scene the prophet Micaiah describes in 1 Kings 22:19 to 22. Other readers hear a royal way of speaking, or, in many Christian readings, a hint of the Trinity.

The seraphim's song did not stay in Isaiah's book. Jewish prayer services still repeat it in a prayer called the Kedushah. Many Christian services sing it in the Sanctus. In this chapter you will look closely at the names the Bible gives to heavenly beings like these, and at what those names tell you.
story.think: The seraphim cover their faces even while standing near God. What might that detail be meant to show a reader about them?

lessons.title: Angel Is a Job Title
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew and Greek words for angel both mean messenger, so the word names a job, not a kind of being.
reading: Open Genesis 32. In verse 1, Jacob is traveling, and "the angels of God" meet him. Two verses later, Jacob sends "messengers" ahead to his brother Esau. English uses two different words. The Hebrew uses one word both times: *mal'ak*, plural mal'akim. Jacob's messengers were ordinary men. The beings who met him were from God. The word is the same because both groups do the same task. They carry a message.

Greek works the same way. The New Testament word is *angelos*, and it too means messenger. Mark 1:2 uses it for John the Baptist, a human being. The last book of the Old Testament is called Malachi, which means "my messenger" in Hebrew. So when readers see "angel" in an English Bible, the older languages are usually saying "one who is sent." Translators decide from the context whether the messenger is human or heavenly.

Ancient readers noticed this too. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of the first century CE, wrote that the beings other philosophers called daemons, Moses called angels. He pictured them as souls living in the air (On the Giants, C. D. Yonge's translation). In his book Angels (2018), Michael Heiser built on the language point. He argued that some biblical terms describe a being's role, while others describe its status or its home. Angel, in his reading, is a role word. It tells you what a being is doing, not what kind of being it is. Other scholars make the same language point, even when they read particular passages differently.

words.d: Hebrew for messenger; used for both human and heavenly messengers
Greek for messenger; the source of the English word angel
a term that names what a being does, such as messenger, rather than what it is

look.title: One Word, Two Kinds of Messenger
look.text: Genesis 32:1: Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him. Genesis 32:3: Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to Esau his brother. In Hebrew, "angels" and "messengers" here are the same word, mal'akim.
look.prompt: If you only had the Hebrew word, how would you decide which messengers were human and which were heavenly? What clues in each verse help?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word mal'ak mean?
check.why: Mal'ak means messenger. Genesis 32 uses it for heavenly beings and for Jacob's human messengers.

check.q: Why does Genesis 32 use the same Hebrew word for God's angels and Jacob's messengers?
choices: Because Jacob's messengers were secretly angels
Because the Hebrew language had only one word for any person
Because the verse was copied wrongly
Because both groups carry out the same task of bringing a message
check.why: The word names a task. Both groups are sent with a message, so both are mal'akim.

check.q: In Angels (2018), how did Heiser describe the word angel?
choices: As the highest rank of heavenly being
As a word used only in the New Testament
As a name for people who have died
As a word for a being's role or job
check.why: Heiser treated angel as a role word. It tells what a being does, carrying messages, not what kind of being it is.

lessons.title: Elohim, Sons of God, Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Elohim, sons of God and holy ones are words that place beings in the unseen realm around God.
reading: Psalm 82:1 reads, in the King James Version, "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods." In Hebrew, both "God" and "gods" are the same word: *elohim*. The God of Israel is called elohim. So are the members of his council. So, once, is the spirit of the dead Samuel in 1 Samuel 28:13. Heiser argued that elohim is not a name for one particular being. It is a word for any being whose natural home is the spirit world.

Another phrase is *sons of God*. In Job 1:6 and 2:1 the sons of God come to present themselves before the LORD. In Job 38:7 they shout for joy when the earth's foundations are laid. Clay tablets from ancient Ugarit, in Syria, speak of a council of the gods around the high god El. E. Theodore Mullen compared that council with Israel's in The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature (1980). Many readers agree the sons of God in Job are heavenly beings. Genesis 6, where the phrase also appears, is more debated.

A third term is *holy ones*, in Hebrew qedoshim. Psalm 89:5 to 7 speaks of an assembly of the holy ones in the heavens. It asks who among the heavenly beings can compare to the LORD. Holy means set apart. All three terms describe status: where a being belongs and how it stands near God. They say little about what job it is doing at a given moment. That is what role words like messenger do.

words.d: Hebrew word used for God, for the gods of the council and for other beings of the spirit world
a phrase in Job and elsewhere for heavenly beings in God's household
Hebrew qedoshim; heavenly beings set apart, gathered in God's assembly
a term that says where a being belongs or how it ranks, not what task it is doing

look.title: The Assembly of the Holy Ones
look.text: For who in the heaven can be compared unto the LORD? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the LORD? God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him.
look.prompt: The word translated "saints" here is qedoshim, holy ones. Who does the psalm say is in this assembly, and where is it?

check.q: In Psalm 82:1, which Hebrew word is translated both "God" and "gods"?
check.why: Psalm 82:1 uses elohim for the God of Israel and for the members of his council.

check.q: According to Heiser, what does the word elohim mark?
choices: A being whose natural home is the spirit world
check.why: Heiser argued elohim is a word for any being of the spirit world, which is why it can name God, the council and even Samuel's spirit.

check.q: In Job 38:7, what do the sons of God do?
choices: They carry the ark of the covenant
They shout for joy as the earth is founded
They guard the garden of Eden
check.why: Job 38:7 says the morning stars sang together and the sons of God shouted for joy when the earth's foundations were laid.

lessons.title: Host, Ministers and Watchers
lessons.mainIdea: Host, ministers and watchers name the heavenly beings as an army, as servants and as those who keep watch.
reading: In 1 Kings 22:19 the prophet Micaiah says he saw the LORD on his throne with "all the host of heaven" standing on his right and his left. The word *host* translates the Hebrew tsaba, a word for an army. The title "LORD of hosts" appears hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible. Isaiah's seraphim use it. In Luke 2:13 a "multitude of the heavenly host" praises God over the shepherds. The picture is of a great, ordered company around a king.

Psalm 103:20 to 21 calls on the angels and hosts to bless the LORD. It calls them "ministers of his, that do his pleasure." The word *ministers* here means servants who attend a king. Psalm 104:4 says God makes his ministers a flaming fire, and Hebrews 1:7 quotes that verse. These words describe what the heavenly beings do. They serve and carry out orders. In that sense they are role words, like messenger.

Daniel 4 adds an unusual term. King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of "a watcher and an holy one" coming down from heaven (4:13). A decision is said to come "by the decree of the watchers" (4:17). This part of Daniel is in Aramaic, and the word is 'ir, plural 'irin, meaning one who is awake. The watchers in Daniel are God's faithful servants. In 1976 J. T. Milik published the Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch found in Qumran Cave 4. They use the same word for the Watchers who sinned. So the word by itself does not mean good or bad. The story around it does.

words.d: from Hebrew tsaba, an army; the whole company of heavenly beings around God
servants who attend a king; used for heavenly beings in Psalms 103 and 104
Aramaic 'ir, one who is awake; a heavenly being in Daniel 4 and in 1 Enoch

look.title: The Decree of the Watchers
look.text: This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.
look.prompt: The watchers and holy ones announce a decision here. According to the verse, who really rules, and what are the watchers doing?

check.q: The Hebrew word tsaba, translated "host," first of all means what?
check.why: Tsaba is a word for an army. "LORD of hosts" pictures God as commander of a heavenly company.

check.q: In which book does a watcher and a holy one come down from heaven in a king's dream?
check.why: Daniel 4:13 tells of Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a watcher and a holy one coming down from heaven.

check.q: What does the word watcher, by itself, tell a reader?
choices: Nothing about whether it is good or bad
That the being appears only in the New Testament
That the being is a human prophet
check.why: Daniel 4's watchers are faithful, while the Aramaic Enoch fragments use the same word for Watchers who sinned. The story decides, not the word.

lessons.title: Cherubim
lessons.mainIdea: Cherubim in the Bible are guardians of God's presence, not the chubby babies of later art.
reading: The first *cherubim* in the Bible stand at the east of Eden in Genesis 3:24. They guard the way to the tree of life with a flaming sword. In Exodus 25:18 to 22, two golden cherubim are made for the cover of the ark of the covenant. Their wings stretch over it. God says he will meet Moses and speak with him from between them. In both places, cherubim guard the space where God is present.

Ezekiel 1 describes four living creatures beneath a throne-chariot. Each has four faces and four wings. In Ezekiel 10:20 the prophet says he knew these were cherubim. Many scholars compare them to the winged guardian figures of the ancient Near East. The Assyrian kings, for example, set huge winged creatures with human heads at their palace gates. Read in that setting, the biblical cherubim are throne guardians around a divine king. Philo of Alexandria read them another way. He took the two cherubim of Genesis 3 as symbols of God's two chief powers, goodness and authority (On the Cherubim).

Later art changed the picture. Renaissance painters filled their works with winged baby figures, called *putti*, borrowed from the cupids of Greek and Roman art. Over time people began calling these babies cherubs. Many scholars point out that nothing in Genesis, Exodus or Ezekiel describes cherubim as babies. The texts describe powerful, many-faced beings who guard what is holy.

words.d: Hebrew plural of cherub; winged beings who guard God's presence in Genesis, Exodus and Ezekiel
a being who stands at or beside a king's throne to guard it
winged baby figures in Renaissance art, borrowed from classical cupids

look.title: Three Places Cherubim Stand
look.text: Genesis 3:24: cherubim with a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life. Exodus 25:22: God will speak to Moses from between the two cherubim on the ark. Ezekiel 10:20: the living creatures under God's throne are cherubim.
look.prompt: What do these three places have in common? Write one sentence that describes the job of cherubim across all three texts.

check.q: Where do cherubim first appear in the Bible?
choices: Guarding the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24
At the empty tomb in Matthew 28
check.why: Genesis 3:24 places cherubim east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.

check.q: In Exodus 25, where are the golden cherubim placed?
choices: On the cover of the ark of the covenant
At the gates of the city
At the top of Mount Sinai
check.why: Exodus 25:18-22 places two golden cherubim on the ark's cover, with God speaking from between them.

check.q: Where did the picture of cherubs as winged babies come from?
choices: Renaissance art that borrowed classical cupids
check.why: Renaissance putti were modeled on classical cupids. The biblical texts describe powerful guardians, not babies.

lessons.title: Seraphim
lessons.mainIdea: Seraphim, the burning ones of Isaiah 6, stand above God's throne and call out his holiness.
reading: Isaiah 6 is the only place in the Bible where *seraphim* appear clearly as heavenly beings. They stand above the LORD's throne. Each has six wings. They cover their faces and feet and call out, "Holy, holy, holy." One of them brings a coal from the altar to cleanse Isaiah's lips. They are worshipers and also agents who act.

The Hebrew root saraph is linked to burning. So seraphim can be translated "burning ones." Many readers take this as a picture of fiery brightness around God. But the same word appears elsewhere for serpents. In Numbers 21:6 the LORD sends "fiery serpents" among the people, and the Hebrew there is seraphim. Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6 mention a flying saraph.

Heiser noted this link. He argued that the seraphim may have been pictured as shining, serpent-like throne guardians. Egyptian royal art often shows cobras, called *uraeus* serpents, guarding a king. Other scholars prefer to keep the image simpler, as glowing beings with human-like faces, feet and hands. The text of Isaiah 6 gives faces, feet and wings, and leaves the rest to the reader.

words.d: Hebrew plural of seraph, burning ones; the six-winged beings above God's throne in Isaiah 6
Hebrew root linked to burning; also used for serpents in Numbers 21 and Isaiah
the upright cobra shown guarding Egyptian kings in ancient art

look.title: Wings in the Throne Visions
look.prompt: Which text's creatures look most like Isaiah's seraphim by wing count? What else might Revelation 4 borrow from Isaiah 6?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word seraphim most likely mean?
check.why: Seraphim comes from a root linked to burning, so it is often translated burning ones.

check.q: Where else does the Hebrew word seraphim appear, used for serpents?
check.why: Numbers 21:6 calls the snakes sent among the people seraphim, fiery serpents.

check.q: How did Heiser's reading of the seraphim differ from a simpler reading?
choices: He said they were human priests
He said they had no wings
He suggested they were pictured as serpent-like throne guardians
He said Isaiah 6 was about Egypt
check.why: Heiser pointed to the serpent meaning of saraph and to Egyptian cobra guardians. Other scholars picture glowing beings with human features.

lessons.title: Living Creatures in Revelation
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 4 draws on both Ezekiel and Isaiah for its four living creatures around God's throne.
reading: In Revelation 4:6 to 8, John sees four *living creatures* around God's throne. One is like a lion, one like a calf, one has a face like a man, and one is like a flying eagle. Each has six wings and is full of eyes. Day and night they say, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come."

Readers who know the Hebrew Bible notice the echoes. The four faces of lion, ox, man and eagle come from Ezekiel 1:10, where each creature has all four. The six wings and the triple "holy" come from Isaiah 6. Revelation blends the two visions into one scene. This kind of borrowing is called *allusion*. A writer brings in older texts so that readers will recall them.

Many scholars read Revelation 4 as another picture of God's throne room, with the council setting found in 1 Kings 22 and Daniel 7. Christian tradition from the late 100s onward also linked the four faces to the four Gospels. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, made one such pairing in Against Heresies, Book 3 (Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1). Later writers, such as Jerome, paired them differently. These links are readings of the symbols, not something Revelation itself states.

words.d: the four beings around God's throne in Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4
a brief reference that calls an earlier text to the reader's mind
the scene of God seated as king, surrounded by heavenly beings

look.title: Two Visions Blended
look.text: Ezekiel 1: four creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) and four wings. Isaiah 6: seraphim with six wings calling "Holy, holy, holy." Revelation 4: four creatures, each with one face (lion, calf, man, eagle), six wings, calling "Holy, holy, holy."
look.prompt: List two details Revelation takes from Ezekiel and two it takes from Isaiah. Why might John's vision bring both older visions together?

check.q: How many wings does each living creature have in Revelation 4:8?
check.why: Revelation 4:8 gives each creature six wings, like the seraphim of Isaiah 6.

check.q: Which older text supplies the four faces of lion, ox, man and eagle?
check.why: Ezekiel 1:10 gives each living creature the faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle.

check.q: Linking the four faces to the four Gospels is best described as what?
choices: A rule from the Dead Sea Scrolls
A later Christian reading of the symbols
check.why: Irenaeus and later writers made the Gospel pairings. Revelation itself does not state them.

sections.title: Ranks in the Text and Beyond

lessons.title: Archangels and Named Angels
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible uses the word archangel only twice, and names very few angels, but later Jewish writings name more.
reading: The word *archangel* means chief angel. It appears only twice in the New Testament. 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says the Lord will come down "with the voice of the archangel." Jude 9 calls Michael "the archangel" and tells of his dispute with the devil over the body of Moses. In Daniel 10:13 Michael is "one of the chief princes," and in Daniel 12:1 he is "the great prince" who stands for Daniel's people.

Only two angels are named in the Protestant Bible. Michael appears in Daniel, Jude and Revelation 12:7. *Gabriel* explains visions to Daniel in Daniel 8 and 9. In Luke 1 he announces the births of John and Jesus. The book of Tobit, which is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, names Raphael. There he calls himself one of seven holy angels who stand before God (12:15).

Jewish writings from the Second Temple period name more. 1 Enoch 20, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, lists holy angels who watch. They include Uriel, Raphael, Michael and Gabriel. 1 Enoch 40 names four angels who stand before God: Michael, Raphael, Gabriel and Phanuel. George Nickelsburg's commentary, 1 Enoch 1 (2001), traces how such lists grew. Many readers see them as developing hints in the Bible, such as Daniel's chief princes. A careful reader notices the difference between what the canonical texts say and what later writers added.

words.d: chief angel; used in the New Testament only in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Jude 9
the angel called a chief prince in Daniel and the archangel in Jude 9
the angel who explains visions to Daniel and announces births in Luke 1
the era of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, about 516 BCE to 70 CE

look.title: Angels Named in the Protestant Bible
look.cite: Michael: Daniel 10:13, 10:21, 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7. Gabriel: Daniel 8:16, 9:21; Luke 1:19, 1:26
look.prompt: Raphael and Uriel are well known today. Which ancient books name them, if the Protestant Bible does not?

check.q: Which New Testament verse calls Michael the archangel?
check.why: Jude 9 names "Michael the archangel" disputing with the devil about the body of Moses.

check.q: In which book does Raphael call himself one of seven holy angels?
check.why: Tobit 12:15 has Raphael say he is one of the seven holy angels. Tobit is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

check.q: What does Daniel 10:13 call Michael?
check.why: Daniel 10:13 calls Michael one of the chief princes, a hint of rank that later writers built on.

lessons.title: Nine Choirs: A Later System
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's words for powers hint at ranks, but the nine choirs of angels come from a writer about 500 CE.
reading: Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through Christ, "whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers." Ephesians 1:21 lists principality, power, might and dominion. These are words for rulers and their territories. Paul does not arrange them into a ladder. Clinton Arnold, in Powers of Darkness (1992), read them as spiritual powers, as Jewish writings of the time did. Walter Wink, in Naming the Powers (1984), argued that the words cover both heavenly powers and earthly rulers and institutions.

About 500 CE a Christian writer produced a book called The Celestial Hierarchy. He wrote under the name of Dionysius, a man Paul met in Athens (Acts 17:34). Scholars call him *Pseudo-Dionysius*, since the real author lived centuries later. He arranged angels into nine orders, often called the nine *choirs*, in three groups of three. Seraphim, cherubim and thrones came first. Dominions, powers and authorities came next. Principalities, archangels and angels came last. Translations name the middle group in slightly different ways.

This system shaped later thought. Thomas Aquinas discussed it, and Dante's Paradiso pictures the nine orders circling God. Catholic and Orthodox traditions still use it. Many Protestant readers see it as a thoughtful guess that goes beyond the text. Readers who start with the terms in the Bible mark the full ranking as a later *hierarchy* built on them.

words.d: rulers; one of Paul's words for heavenly powers in Colossians and Ephesians
the unknown author, about 500 CE, of The Celestial Hierarchy, writing under an earlier name
the nine orders of angels in Pseudo-Dionysius's system
a system that ranks members from highest to lowest

look.title: Text and System Side by Side
look.text: Colossians 1:16 names four kinds of powers: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers. Pseudo-Dionysius, about 500 CE, lists nine orders in three groups: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, powers, authorities; principalities, archangels, angels.
look.prompt: Which names in the nine choirs come from Paul, and which come from other Bible books? What did Pseudo-Dionysius add that neither source states?

check.q: About when did Pseudo-Dionysius write The Celestial Hierarchy?
check.why: The Celestial Hierarchy is dated to about 500 CE, centuries after the real Dionysius of Acts 17.

check.q: How did Walter Wink read Paul's power words in Naming the Powers (1984)?
choices: As the nine choirs in order
As other names for the Watchers of Daniel 4
As words covering both heavenly powers and earthly rulers and institutions
As names for church leaders only
check.why: Wink argued the power words cover heavenly and earthly rulers together. Clinton Arnold stressed their spiritual sense.

check.q: Why is the author called Pseudo-Dionysius?
choices: He wrote under the name of a much earlier figure from Acts 17
check.why: He wrote as Dionysius, whom Paul met in Athens, but lived centuries later. Pseudo means false name.

lessons.title: Guardian Angels?
lessons.mainIdea: A few verses link angels to believers, and traditions differ on how far to take the idea of a personal guardian.
reading: In Matthew 18:10 Jesus says not to despise "these little ones," because "in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father." In Acts 12, Peter is freed from prison and knocks at the door of Mary's house. A servant named Rhoda runs to tell the others. They answer, "It is his angel" (12:15). Psalm 91:11 says God will give his angels charge over the one who trusts him.

Many Christians read these verses as teaching that each believer has a *guardian angel*. An early Christian book, the Shepherd of Hermas, says each person has two angels, one of righteousness and one of wickedness (Mandate 6.2, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 2). The Catholic Church teaches that each believer has an angel as protector and keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2. The Talmud (Shabbat 119b) tells of two ministering angels who walk a person home on the eve of the Sabbath.

Careful readers separate what these verses say from what later teaching builds on them. Matthew 18:10 says the little ones have angels who see God's face. It does not say how many angels or what they do. Acts 12:15 tells what Peter's friends believed. It is a report of their words, not a separate teaching. The Sabbath song Shalom Aleichem greets the angels of the Talmud's story. Careful readers weigh each verse on its own before building a doctrine.

words.d: an angel believed to watch over a particular person
a large collection of Jewish legal and teaching discussions, completed about 500 to 600 CE
a teaching that a religious community holds and passes on

look.title: Their Angels in Heaven
look.text: Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
look.prompt: What exactly does this verse say about the little ones' angels? Make two lists: what the verse states, and what readers have added.

check.q: In Acts 12:15, who do Peter's friends think is at the door?
check.why: When Rhoda says Peter is at the door, the others answer, "It is his angel."

check.q: Which tradition keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2?
check.why: The Catholic Church teaches that each believer has a guardian angel and keeps a feast for them on October 2.

check.q: What does Matthew 18:10 say the little ones' angels do?
choices: Always see the face of the Father in heaven
Carry them to heaven when they die
check.why: The verse says their angels always behold the face of the Father. It says nothing further about their tasks.

lessons.title: People Do Not Become Angels
lessons.mainIdea: In the Bible, angels and humans are different kinds of beings, and the texts do not say the dead become angels.
reading: In the 1946 film It's a Wonderful Life, a man who died long ago returns as Clarence, "Angel, Second Class," trying to earn his wings. Many people today say that someone who has died has become an angel. Heiser pointed out that this is a popular idea, not a biblical one. In the Bible, angels and humans are different kinds of beings.

Several texts support his point. Job 38:7 has the sons of God shouting for joy when the earth was founded, before any humans existed. In Matthew 22:30 Jesus says the raised dead will be "as the angels" in not marrying. The word as makes a comparison. It does not say they become angels. Hebrews 12:22 to 23 lists "an innumerable company of angels" and, separately, "the spirits of just men made perfect." The two groups stand side by side.

Heiser also drew on 1 Corinthians 6:3, where Paul says believers will judge angels. In his reading, the New Testament pictures redeemed humans raised to share in God's rule, as humans, even above the angels. Other Christian readers stress different parts of these texts, but most agree on the basic *distinction* between human and angel. The popular idea often grows from grief and love for someone who has died.

words.d: a clear difference between two things
being raised from death to a new bodily life, as the New Testament describes it
a belief widely held in a culture that may not come from the source texts

look.title: "As the Angels"
look.text: Matthew 22:30: in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. Hebrews 12:22-23: the heavenly Jerusalem holds an innumerable company of angels, the church of the firstborn, God the Judge of all, and the spirits of just men made perfect.
look.prompt: Does either text say that people become angels? Point to the exact words that show how the writer compares or separates the two.

check.q: Which verse has the sons of God shouting for joy before humans existed?
check.why: Job 38:7 places the sons of God at the founding of the earth, before people were made.

check.q: In Matthew 22:30, what does Jesus say about the raised dead?
choices: They are as the angels in not marrying
check.why: Jesus compares them to angels in one way, not marrying. The word as makes a comparison, not a change of kind.

check.q: How does Hebrews 12:22-23 show that angels and humans are distinct?
choices: It says angels were once humans
It names Michael as a human prophet
It says the dead earn wings
It lists angels and the spirits of just men as separate groups
check.why: Hebrews 12:22-23 names the company of angels and the spirits of just men side by side, as two groups.

lessons.title: The Son Above the Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Hebrews 1 and 2 argue from the Hebrew Bible that the Son is greater than the angels.
reading: The letter to the Hebrews opens with an argument about angels. Hebrews 1:4 says the Son has become "so much better than the angels." Then the writer strings together quotations from the Hebrew Bible. Hebrews 1:5 asks to which angel God ever said, "Thou art my Son" (Psalm 2:7). Hebrews 1:14 calls angels "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation."

Hebrews 1:6 says, "let all the angels of God worship him." This line is not in the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, the *Masoretic Text*. It matches Deuteronomy 32:43 in the *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation, as Brenton's 1844 English version shows. A Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4 has a similar line. Scholars of the text point to cases like this, where the New Testament follows an older form of the text.

Hebrews 2:7 quotes Psalm 8, where humans are made "a little lower than the angels." The Hebrew of Psalm 8:5 has elohim there, and the Septuagint rendered it angels. Hebrews 2:5 adds that the world to come is not put under angels. Most Christian readers take these chapters as showing the Son's rank over the whole heavenly host. Scholars differ on why the writer needed to argue it so strongly.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, preserved by Jewish scribes in the Middle Ages
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the 200s BCE
Hebrews 1:14's description of angels as servants sent to help

look.title: Ministering Spirits
look.text: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?
look.prompt: Is this verse describing what angels are, what they do, or both? Use the ideas of status words and role words.

check.q: Where does the line "let all the angels of God worship him" in Hebrews 1:6 come from?
check.why: The line matches the Greek Septuagint of Deuteronomy 32:43. A Dead Sea Scrolls copy has a similar Hebrew line.

check.q: In Psalm 8:5, which Hebrew word did the Septuagint translate as angels?
check.why: Psalm 8:5 in Hebrew has elohim. The Septuagint rendered it angels, and Hebrews 2:7 quotes that form.

check.q: What does Hebrews 1:14 call angels?
choices: Rulers of the world to come
check.why: Hebrews 1:14 calls them ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation.

review.q: Which pair shows the difference between a role word and a status word?
review.why: Messenger (mal'ak) names a job. Elohim names a being's home in the spirit world, a status.

review.q: Who sees seraphim calling "Holy, holy, holy" above the LORD's throne?
review.why: Isaiah 6 tells the prophet's vision of the seraphim in the year King Uzziah died.

review.q: How do readers differ on the "us" in Isaiah 6:8?
choices: Many hear God speaking before his council; others hear a royal way of speaking or a hint of the Trinity
Some call it a copying error; others say it is poetry
Some say it means the seraphim only; others say the people
Some say it means Isaiah and the king; others say the priests
review.why: Many scholars read "us" as God addressing his council, as in 1 Kings 22. Others hear a royal plural or, in many Christian readings, the Trinity.

review.q: Which beings guard the ark's cover in Exodus 25?
review.why: Exodus 25:18-22 describes two golden cherubim over the ark's cover.

review.q: The word watcher in Daniel 4 is Aramaic. Which later writing uses the same word for beings who sinned?
review.why: The Aramaic copies of 1 Enoch use 'irin for the Watchers who sinned. Daniel's watchers are faithful.

review.q: Which statement about the nine choirs of angels is accurate?
choices: They are listed in order in Colossians 1:16
They come from Pseudo-Dionysius, about 500 CE
review.why: The nine choirs come from The Celestial Hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius. Paul names some powers but gives no ranked list.

review.q: Which idea is popular today but not found in the Bible's texts?
review.why: The texts treat angels and humans as different kinds of beings. Hebrews 12:22-23 lists them as separate groups.

review.q: How does Hebrews 1 argue that the Son is greater than the angels?
choices: By telling a new vision of heaven
By quoting passages from the Hebrew Bible, some in their Septuagint form
review.why: Hebrews 1 builds its case from quotations such as Psalm 2:7 and Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Septuagint.

chapters.title: Angels in Worship, Law and Story
chapters.bigQuestion: What jobs do angels do in the Bible's stories, and why do the texts insist that they are never to be worshiped?

story.title: Get Up, I Am a Servant Too
story.kicker: Near the end of Revelation, John falls at an angel's feet, and the angel tells him to stop.
paragraphs: The book of Revelation says it was written by a man named John on the island of Patmos, off the coast of what is now Turkey (Revelation 1:9). It is full of visions. John sees thrones, lampstands, sealed scrolls and a city of gold. Angels guide him through much of it. They show him scenes and explain what they mean.

In Revelation 19, an angel tells John to write down a blessing on those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John is overwhelmed. He falls at the angel's feet to worship him. The angel stops him at once: "See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God."

Then, near the very end of the book, it happens again. In Revelation 22:8 to 9, John says that when he had heard and seen these things, he fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who showed them to him. The angel gives almost the same answer. He is a fellow servant with John, with the prophets and with all who keep the words of the book. Worship God.

Readers have long noticed that the scene appears twice. Some think the repetition is there on purpose, to make the lesson impossible to miss. The angel does not scold John or frighten him. He simply puts himself on the same level as John, as a servant, and points away from himself.

Many readers treat scenes like this as a key to how the Bible talks about angels. They are powerful and they serve, but worship is for God alone. In this chapter you will follow angels through the giving of the law, the worship of heaven, the Gospel stories and later Jewish writings, and see how that key keeps turning up.
story.think: The angel calls himself John's fellow servant. What does that phrase say about how the angel sees himself compared to John?

lessons.title: A Fiery Law and Holy Ones
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 33:2 links Sinai with God's holy ones, and the Greek Septuagint names angels there directly.
reading: Exodus 19 and 20 tell of God giving the law at Mount *Sinai* with thunder, fire and a thick cloud. Those chapters do not mention angels. But a later poem does. In Deuteronomy 33:2, Moses blesses the tribes and says that the LORD came from Sinai. In the King James Version, he came "with ten thousands of saints," and from his right hand went "a fiery law." The Hebrew for saints here is qedoshim, holy ones.

The Hebrew of this verse is hard. The words translated "fiery law" are unusual, and scholars still debate them. The *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation made in the centuries before Jesus, reads the end of the verse differently. It says that at God's right hand there were angels with him. So in the Greek, the angels at Sinai are named outright. A difference like this between two forms of a text is called a *variant*.

Psalm 68:17 adds another picture. It says the chariots of God are twenty thousand, and the Lord is among them, as in Sinai. Heiser read these verses together. In his view, the Hebrew Bible pictures God at Sinai surrounded by his heavenly host, and the Septuagint made that picture plainer. Other scholars read the Hebrew holy ones as possibly Israel's own people, or stress how uncertain the verse is.

words.d: the mountain where, in Exodus, God gives Israel the law
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the 200s BCE
a difference in wording between two copies or versions of the same text

look.title: The LORD Came From Sinai
look.text: The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them.
look.prompt: The Greek Septuagint ends this verse with angels at God's right hand. Which words in the English here might a reader connect with angels, and why?

check.q: Which version of Deuteronomy 33:2 names angels with God directly?
check.why: The Septuagint says angels were at God's right hand. The Hebrew speaks of holy ones and a hard phrase often read as fiery law.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word behind "saints" in Deuteronomy 33:2 mean?
check.why: The Hebrew is qedoshim, holy ones, the same word used for God's heavenly assembly in Psalm 89.

check.q: What is a variant?
choices: A difference in wording between versions of a text
A song sung in the temple
check.why: A variant is a place where two copies or versions of a text read differently, like the Hebrew and Greek of Deuteronomy 33:2.

lessons.title: The Law Given Through Angels
lessons.mainIdea: Three New Testament passages say the law came through angels, a tradition shared with other Jewish writings of the time.
reading: In Acts 7, Stephen speaks before the council in Jerusalem. He ends by saying his hearers "received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it" (7:53). Paul writes in Galatians 3:19 that the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a *mediator*." Hebrews 2:2 calls the law "the word spoken by angels." Three different writers assume the same thing. Angels had a part in giving the law at Sinai.

This idea was not new with the New Testament. The book of *Jubilees*, written in Hebrew around the 100s BCE, retells Genesis and part of Exodus. In it, an angel of the presence writes out history for Moses on the mountain (Jubilees 1:27 to 2:1, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation). Jubilees is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Josephus, writing in the 90s CE, has King Herod tell his troops that the Jews learned the holiest part of their laws from God through angels (Antiquities 15.5.3, Whiston's 1737 translation). Scholars debate whether Herod means heavenly angels or human messengers such as prophets.

Many scholars think the New Testament writers drew on this shared *tradition*, which grew from verses like Deuteronomy 33:2. Readers differ on why each writer mentions it. In Galatians, many scholars think Paul uses it to say the law came less directly than God's promise to Abraham. In Hebrews, the point is that if the word spoken by angels was binding, the message spoken by the Son matters even more.

words.d: a go-between who carries terms or words between two parties
a Jewish retelling of Genesis and Exodus from about the 100s BCE; canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church
beliefs and stories handed down within a community over time

look.title: Three Writers, One Tradition
look.text: Acts 7:53: you received the law by the disposition of angels. Galatians 3:19: the law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Hebrews 2:2: the word spoken by angels was steadfast.
look.prompt: Each writer mentions angels and the law for a different purpose. Pick one verse, read the verses around it, and explain what point the writer is making.

check.q: Who says in Acts 7:53 that the law was received by the disposition of angels?
check.why: Stephen says this at the end of his speech before the council in Acts 7.

check.q: In Josephus's Antiquities 15.5.3, what does Herod tell his troops?
choices: That angels must be worshiped before battle
That the Jews learned their holiest laws from God through angels
check.why: Josephus has Herod say the holiest laws came from God through angels. Scholars debate whether he means heavenly or human messengers.

check.q: What point do many scholars think Paul makes in Galatians 3:19?
choices: That the law was never given
That the law came less directly than God's promise to Abraham
check.why: Paul contrasts the law, given through angels and a mediator, with the promise God spoke directly to Abraham.

lessons.title: "See Thou Do It Not"
lessons.mainIdea: In Revelation, an angel twice refuses John's worship and calls himself a fellow servant.
reading: In Revelation 19:10 and again in 22:8 to 9, John falls down before an angel to *worship* him. Both times the angel stops him. He says he is John's *fellowservant*. He is a servant like John, the prophets and all who keep the words of the book. Both times he ends with two words: worship God.

The angel's answer rests on an old command. Exodus 20:3 says, "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." The Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4 calls Israel to love the LORD alone. The angel is glorious and has just shown John great visions. Even so, the text puts him on John's side of the line, among those who serve, and not among those who receive worship.

Heiser pointed to these scenes to show that the heavenly host serves God and does not share his place. He argued that the Bible can call heavenly beings elohim and still hold that only one elohim, the God of Israel, is to be worshiped. Jewish and Christian readers of every kind have read these scenes as a clear warning against giving worship to angels.

words.d: honor and devotion given to God, often shown by bowing or kneeling
one who serves the same master; the angel's word for himself in Revelation 19 and 22
Deuteronomy 6:4-9, a central Jewish declaration that the LORD is one

look.title: Worship God
look.text: And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.
look.prompt: List the three groups the angel says he belongs with. What do those groups have in common?

check.q: What does the angel call himself when he stops John?
check.why: In Revelation 19:10 and 22:9 the angel says, "I am thy fellowservant."

check.q: How many times in Revelation does John fall down to worship an angel?
check.why: It happens in Revelation 19:10 and again in Revelation 22:8-9.

check.q: Which older command does the angel's answer rest on?
choices: Thou shalt have no other gods before me
Honor thy father and thy mother
check.why: Exodus 20:3 forbids having other gods. The angel points John to worship God alone.

lessons.title: Colossians 2:18: Two Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Colossians 2:18 warns about the worship of angels, and scholars read the phrase in two main ways.
reading: Paul's letter to the Colossians warns its readers about teachers who were judging them. In the King James Version, Colossians 2:18 says, "Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen." The key phrase in Greek is thrēskeia tōn angelōn, "worship of the angels."

The phrase is *ambiguous*, meaning it can be read more than one way. In the first reading, it means worship given to angels. Some people in Colossae, on this view, were honoring angels in a way the letter rejects. In the second reading, it means the worship that angels offer. On this view, some teachers claimed to join the angels' worship in heaven through visions, and looked down on those who did not.

Both readings have strong defenders. The second reading gained support after the Dead Sea Scrolls showed Jewish groups who hoped to join the worship of angels. Either way, the letter's answer is the same. Colossians 2:19 says the readers should hold fast to the head, which in this letter is Christ. On both readings, the letter keeps angels in a serving role, never sharing God's worship.

words.d: able to be read in more than one way
an ancient town in what is now western Turkey, home of the church Colossians addresses
a scene seen in a dream or trance, often reported as coming from God

look.title: Worship of the Angels
look.text: Reading 1: the Colossians were being urged to give worship to angels. Reading 2: some teachers claimed, through visions, to join in the worship the angels offer in heaven. The Greek phrase is the same in both: worship of the angels.
look.prompt: Which words in Colossians 2:18, such as "intruding into those things which he hath not seen," might support each reading? Explain one.

check.q: In the second reading of Colossians 2:18, what does "worship of angels" mean?
choices: Worship that people give to angels
The worship that angels themselves offer in heaven
check.why: The second reading takes the phrase as the angels' own worship, which some teachers claimed to join through visions.

check.q: What discovery gave support to the second reading?
check.why: The Dead Sea Scrolls show Jewish groups who hoped to join the worship of angels, which made the second reading more likely to some scholars.

check.q: What does ambiguous mean?
choices: Able to be read in more than one way
check.why: An ambiguous phrase can fairly be read more than one way, like worship of the angels in Colossians 2:18.

lessons.title: Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
lessons.mainIdea: A Dead Sea Scrolls text pictures angels as priests leading worship in a heavenly temple.
reading: In caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea, scholars found copies of a work now called the *Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice*. More copies turned up at Masada, the desert fortress. The work has thirteen songs, one for each of the first thirteen Sabbaths of the year. The copies date from about the first century BCE to the first century CE.

The songs do not describe worship on earth. They call on heavenly beings to praise God in a heavenly *sanctuary*. The songs call these beings elohim, holy ones and chief princes. They describe them as priests who serve before God. Later songs picture the heavenly temple itself, its chariot-throne and its cherubim, joining in praise. The people who sang these songs seem to have hoped their worship on earth matched the worship above.

The Songs help readers see the Jewish world around the New Testament. They show how Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 were read and expanded. Carol Newsom published the first full edition of the Songs, Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice: A Critical Edition (1985). The Songs also show why some scholars read Colossians 2:18 as being about joining the angels' worship. The singers praise God alongside the angels. They do not worship the angels themselves.

words.d: a Dead Sea Scrolls work of thirteen songs describing angels' worship in heaven
the site by the Dead Sea near the caves where most of the Dead Sea Scrolls were found
a holy place for worship; here, the heavenly temple

look.title: Where the Copies Were Found
look.cite: Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice: 4Q400-407, 11Q17, and the Masada copy; standard scholarly counts
look.prompt: What does finding ten copies in two places suggest about how the Songs were used?

check.q: How many songs are in the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice?
check.why: The work has thirteen songs, one for each of the first thirteen Sabbaths of the year.

check.q: How do the Songs describe the angels?
choices: As priests who serve in a heavenly sanctuary
check.why: The Songs call the heavenly beings elohim and chief princes and describe them as priests serving before God.

check.q: Besides Qumran, where were copies of the Songs found?
check.why: A copy of the Songs was also found at Masada, the desert fortress by the Dead Sea.

lessons.title: Messengers at the Births
lessons.mainIdea: In Matthew and Luke, angels bring news of the births of John and Jesus, often starting with "Fear not."
reading: Luke's Gospel opens in the Jerusalem temple. An angel appears to an old priest named Zechariah beside the altar of incense. He says he is *Gabriel*, who stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). He announces that Zechariah's wife Elizabeth will have a son, John. Six months later, Gabriel goes to Nazareth and tells a young woman named Mary that she will bear a son, Jesus (Luke 1:26 to 38). This scene is called the *Annunciation*.

Then, outside Bethlehem, an angel of the Lord appears to shepherds at night. He tells them a Savior is born. Suddenly a multitude of the heavenly host appears, praising God (Luke 2:8 to 14). Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side. An angel of the Lord speaks to Joseph three times in dreams, in Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19. The angel tells him to take Mary as his wife, to flee to Egypt, and to return.

The angels in these stories are messengers in the plain sense of mal'ak and angelos. They bring news and instructions. Again and again they begin with "Fear not." In the Bible, meeting a being from God's presence is overwhelming, and these words calm the hearer. Readers of every tradition have loved these scenes. Christmas music and art have retold them for centuries.

words.d: the angel who announces the births of John and Jesus in Luke 1
the scene in Luke 1:26-38 where Gabriel tells Mary she will bear Jesus
the great company of angels who praise God before the shepherds in Luke 2:13

look.title: Angels in the Birth Stories
look.prompt: Who does the angel speak to in Matthew, and who in Luke? What might that tell you about each writer's focus?

check.q: In Luke 1, to whom does Gabriel first appear?
check.why: Gabriel appears first to the priest Zechariah in the temple, then six months later to Mary.

check.q: In Matthew, how does the angel of the Lord speak to Joseph?
check.why: Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19 all describe an angel speaking to Joseph in a dream.

check.q: What words do the birth-story angels often begin with?
check.why: The angels say "Fear not" to Zechariah, Mary, the shepherds and Joseph, to calm people who are overwhelmed.

lessons.title: Angels at the Empty Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: All four Gospels place heavenly messengers at Jesus' empty tomb, though they describe them differently.
reading: Each Gospel tells of women coming to Jesus' tomb early on the first day of the week. In Matthew 28:2 to 7, an angel of the Lord rolls back the stone and sits on it. His face is like lightning and his clothing white as snow. In Mark 16:5 the women see a young man in a long white robe sitting inside. In Luke 24:4 two men stand by them in shining clothes. In John 20:12, Mary Magdalene sees two angels in white, one at the head and one at the feet of where the body had lain.

Readers have handled these differences in two main ways. Some *harmonize* the accounts, fitting them together into one fuller story. On that view, one writer may simply mention the angel who spoke. Others see each Gospel as passing on its own form of the story, told for its own readers. Both kinds of readers note that the core message is the same in every account. He is not here. He is risen.

The descriptions also show something found across the Bible. Messenger angels often look like men. In Genesis 18, three visitors come to Abraham as travelers. In Mark and Luke, the tomb messengers are called a young man and men, and Luke later calls them angels (24:23). Many readers note that shining clothes and sudden appearing, not wings, are what usually mark these messengers in the text.

words.d: to fit different accounts of one event together into a single story
the Gospels' account of women finding Jesus' burial place open and his body gone
one telling of an event, such as each Gospel's report of the tomb

look.title: Messengers at the Tomb
look.prompt: Two Gospels describe one messenger and two describe two. How might a reader who harmonizes explain this? How might a reader who sees separate forms of the story explain it?

check.q: Which Gospel says an angel rolled back the stone and sat on it?
check.why: Matthew 28:2 says an angel of the Lord rolled back the stone and sat on it.

check.q: What does it mean to harmonize the Gospel accounts?
choices: To fit them together into one fuller story
To choose one and reject the others
check.why: Harmonizing means combining the accounts into a single story, explaining differences as different focus.

check.q: According to the reading, what usually marks messenger angels in the text?
check.why: Messenger angels often look like men, marked by shining clothes and sudden appearing, not by wings.

lessons.title: Raphael in Tobit
lessons.mainIdea: In the book of Tobit, the angel Raphael travels in disguise to help a family and then points them to God.
reading: The book of *Tobit* is a Jewish story probably written around 200 BCE. Copies in Aramaic and Hebrew were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Protestants place it among the *Apocrypha*, books read for learning but not counted as Scripture. It tells of Tobit, a faithful man living in exile in Nineveh, and his son Tobias.

Tobias must make a long journey to collect money his father left in Media. A guide offers to go with him, calling himself Azarias. The two travel together. Along the way the guide helps Tobias catch a fish, arrange his marriage to a young woman named Sarah, and return home safely. At the end, Tobit's eyesight is restored. Only then does the guide reveal who he is.

In Tobit 12, he says he is *Raphael*, one of the seven holy angels who stand before God. His name means "God heals." He tells the family to thank God, not him, and says he came by God's will. He adds that they never truly saw him eat. Tobit shows how Second Temple Jewish writers could picture angels as named, caring messengers who still point beyond themselves to God.

words.d: a Jewish story of about 200 BCE, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, in which Raphael guides a family
books found in some Bibles that Protestants read for learning but do not count as Scripture
the angel in Tobit whose name means God heals

lessons.title: Testing Popular Ideas
lessons.mainIdea: Popular ideas about angels can be tested against what the ancient texts actually say.
reading: Many ideas about angels come from movies, greeting cards and later traditions. A careful reader can go back to the texts and check. Some popular ideas turn out to fit the Bible well. Others add details the Bible never gives. In Angels (2018), Michael Heiser urged readers to sort them by asking, "Which verse says this?"

Here are three examples. First, many people picture every angel with wings. In the texts, the winged beings are mostly cherubim and seraphim. Messengers like the visitors in Genesis 18 or the angel in Judges 13 appear as men. Daniel 9:21 is sometimes read as Gabriel flying, but the Hebrew there is unclear. Second, many people say the dead become angels. Hebrews 12:22 to 23 keeps angels and humans distinct. Third, many think the Bible names many angels. The Protestant Bible names only two.

Heiser also spent years answering the *ancient astronaut* theory. This is the claim that beings from other planets visited early humans and were remembered as gods or angels. Some writers say Ezekiel's vision in Ezekiel 1 describes a spacecraft. Heiser argued that such claims misread the ancient languages. Ezekiel 1:28 itself calls what the prophet saw the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Checking the *context* of a verse is often the quickest test.

words.d: the claim, rejected by Heiser and other scholars, that visitors from other planets were remembered as gods or angels
the words, verses and setting around a passage that shape its meaning
the ideas and images spread by movies, songs, cards and other everyday media

look.title: Check the Claim
look.text: Claim A: every angel has wings. Claim B: a grandparent who dies becomes an angel. Claim C: Ezekiel 1 describes a spacecraft. Tools: Genesis 18:2, Judges 13:6, Hebrews 12:22-23, Ezekiel 1:28.

check.why: Wings are described mostly for cherubim and seraphim. Messenger angels often appear as men.

choices: The likeness of the glory of the LORD

choices: The claim that visitors from other planets were remembered as gods or angels
check.why: The ancient astronaut theory says off-world visitors became the gods of old stories. Scholars of the ancient languages, Heiser among them, reject it.

lessons.title: Angels in Art and Music
lessons.mainIdea: Artists and composers have retold the Bible's angel scenes for centuries, adding details of their own.
reading: Around 1320, the poet Dante finished his Paradiso, the last part of his Divine Comedy. In it he pictures the nine orders of angels circling God in rings of light, following Pseudo-Dionysius. In 1512 the painter Raphael finished the Sistine Madonna. Two small winged children lean on a ledge at the bottom of the painting. These *putti* became some of the most copied angels in the world.

Music carried the angel scenes too. Charles Wesley's Christmas hymn, now known as Hark! The Herald Angels Sing, was first published in 1739. George Frideric Handel composed Messiah in 1741. One of its choruses sets the angels' words from Luke 2:14, "Glory to God in the highest." Choirs in Chicago and around the world still perform Messiah each winter.

Art and music are forms of *interpretation*. Each artist chooses what to show and adds details the text does not give, such as halos, harps, feathered wings or baby faces. A reader can enjoy such works and still know where their details come from. A good habit is to ask of any image: which verse is this showing, and what has the artist added?

words.d: winged baby figures in Renaissance art, often mistaken for biblical cherubim
a way of explaining or showing what a text means
Handel's 1741 musical work setting Bible passages, including the angels' song in Luke 2

One reads Hebrew, one reads Latin
One is about Sinai, one is about the tomb
One says Paul wrote it, one says Peter did

review.why: In Tobit, Raphael, calling himself Azarias, guides Tobias to Media and home again.

An angel sitting on the stone
A vision of the heavenly host singing

choices: Angels giving the law to Moses
Angels guarding the tree of life
Angels serving as priests in a heavenly sanctuary

review.q: Which popular idea about angels comes mostly from Renaissance art?
review.why: Renaissance putti, like those in Raphael's Sistine Madonna, turned cherubs into winged babies. The texts describe guardians.
